Synapsids. A diverse group of amniotes, sometimes called mammal-like reptiles, that dominated terrestrial ecosystems from the Carboniferous through the Permian periods and into the Triassic. They are the ancestors of all mammals, including humans. The synapsid line was the dominant vertebrate group until a mass extinction at the Permian-Triassic boundary devastated them. Understanding synapsids reveals the evolutionary bridge between ancient reptiles and modern mammals.

Synapsids are characterized by a single temporal fenestra, a hole on the skull behind the eye, distinguishing them from sauropsids, which are dinosaurs and living reptiles with a different skull pattern.

Pelycosaurs were early synapsids from the Carboniferous and early Permian periods. They included the sail-backed Dimetrodon, which may have used its sail for thermoregulation or display.

Therapsids were later synapsids, appearing in the Permian and Triassic periods, and were more mammal-like. They showed improved limb posture and jaw structure evolving toward the single mandibular bone of mammals, along with possible insulation via hair.

During the Permian period, synapsids were the apex predators and dominated biomass. Dinosaurs did not become dominant until synapsids were decimated by the Permian-Triassic extinction, approximately 252 million years ago.

Some therapsids like Cynognathus were large, active predators with specialized teeth and forward-facing limbs, suggesting endothermic metabolism, or warm-bloodedness.

Jaw structure evolved incrementally. The reptilian jaw has multiple bones including the quadrate and articular. The mammalian jaw has one: the dentary. Intermediate stages are preserved in the synapsid fossil record. The ear bones of modern mammals—the malleus, incus, and stapes—derived from synapsid jaw bones, evidenced by embryology and fossils.
